text: This magnet is one watt of heat.
It appeared a moment ago, when a server answered a question.
Almost every watt a server uses turns into heat. A single AI rack can give off more than a hundred kilowatts.

text: So, where does the heat go?
First, air carries it off the chips, into a cooling unit.
There, it warms a loop of chilled water, which flows to a chiller.
The chiller hands the heat to a second loop, which climbs up to the roof.
On cold days, the chiller can even switch off, and the roof does the job alone.
Up here is the cooling tower.
Warm water is sprayed over a honeycomb called fill, while a big fan pulls outside air up through it.
asr: Warm water is sprayed over a honeycomb called Phil, while a big fan pulls outside air up through it.

text: A little of the water evaporates, and evaporating water carries a lot of heat away.
Lose about one percent, and the rest comes out around six degrees cooler.
asr: Lose about 1%, and the rest comes out around 6 degrees cooler.
sub: Lose about 1 percent, and the rest comes out around 6 degrees cooler.

text: It's the same trick as sweating, and it uses far less electricity than cooling with air alone.
And our one watt of heat?
What it leaves behind is a water bill.
A big site can evaporate millions of litres a day.
asr: A big sight can evaporate millions of liters a day.

text: So operators measure the litres used for every kilowatt hour, and turn to recycled water where they can.
